ANNUAL CONVENTION TO MARK XI'S
MOTH ANNIVERSARY
WESLEYAN UNIVERSITY, Middletown, Connecticut, was
only twelve
years old when the Xi, the tenth Chapter of
Psi Upsilon to be founded, began its
glorious contribution to local campus and
to national
fraternity life.
The Xi has been represented on the
Executive Council almost continuously
since its estabhshment in 1869. Charles
W. Smiley, '74, served during the period,
1876-84, most of the time as
Secretary and
Treasurer. George S. Coleman, '76, had
the longest tenure, from 1896 to 1921, as
Secretary. A. Avery Hallock, '16, who
served from 1924 to 1937, was Archivist
of the Fraternity from 1930 to the end of
his term on the Council. Robert I. Lag
gren, '13, has been a Council member for
the past six years.
This will be the sixth time that the Xi
has been privileged to be host to the
Annual Convention of Psi Upsilon. The
previous occasions were: 1848, 1865,
1877, 1897, and 1921. The coincidence of
the 120th year of Psi Upsilon, the 110th
Anniversary of the Xi, and the Fortieth
Reunion of one of its most famous delega
tions, augurs a memorable Convention.
An outstanding feature of the Conven
tion will be the honoring of Albert C.
Jacobs, Phi '21, who will be installed in
March as President of Trinity College, the
home of the Beta Beta Chapter, at Hart
ford, Connecticut, just 16 miles from Wes
leyan. Brother Jacobs, at
present Chancel
lor of the University of Denver, and form
erly Provost of Columbia University, is the
son of Albert Poole Jacobs, Phi '73, author
of "The Psi Upsilon Epitome," pubhshed
in 1884, parts of which many of us had
to commit to
memory before initiation.
Brother Al himself was a member of the
Executive Council, 1948-50, and was a
major contributor to and co-editor of the
"Annals of Psi Upsilon," pubhshed in
1941.
Presidents of other New England col
leges who, it is hoped, may be at the
forthcoming Convention are Roswell Gray
Ham, Epsilon '14, President of Mount
Holyoke College and formerly a member
of the Executive Council, and A. V\^hitney
Griswold, Beta '29, President of Yale Uni
versity, alma mater of so
many distin
guished Psi U's. Prescott S. Bush, Beta
'17, newly elected Senator from Connecti
cut, may also be present.
Chairman of the arrangements for the
Convention is Robert I. Laggren, who is
not only a member of the Executive Coun
cil, but a trustee of Wesleyan University.
The vice-chairman is Charles B. Stone,
'23, also a trustee of Wesleyan and VicePresident of the Xi Corporation. Other
officers of the Xi who are
assisting with

ALBERT CHARLES JACOBS. PHI '21, NEW
PRESIDENT OF TRINITY COLLEGE
A
LEADING EDITORIAL in The
Hartford Courant, of Sunday, Oc
tober 19, 1952, reads in part: "Trinity
took a
long time in finding its new
presi
dent. And well it might. For as A. Northey
Jones (Beta Beta '17) of New York, chanman of the selection committee, remarked
during the search, the college will have to
live for some time with its new
president.
Dr. Jacobs was known at Columbia for
his outgiving friendHness, as well as for
the professional competence to which his
record bears witness. Trinity's future is
now in the hands of an educator. The new
president, the college, and the larger com
munity ahke can look forward to a
happy
association." Serving with Brother Jones
on an
eight-man committee on selection of
a new
president, which had investigated
more than 200 recommendations, in a
search extending over a
year and a half,
were Brothers Newton C. Brainard, Beta
'02, chairman of the board of trustees, and
Dr. Jerome P. Webster, Beta Beta '10, an
outstanding plastic surgeon of New York.
Brother Jacobs succeeds G. Keith Funston, who assumed duties as
president of
the New York Stock Exchange in Septem
ber, 1951, after six years as
president of
the 130-year old college of 900 men. It is
expected that installation ceremonies of
Brother Jacobs will take place this coming
Spring.
In returning to New England, Brother
Jacobs is on familiar ground, for his an
cestors settled in Hingham, Mass., in
1636. His mother, Grace W. (Grinnell)
Jacobs, daughter of an
Episcopal minister
in Jackson, Michigan, was a descendant
of Jonathan Edwards. Brother Jacobs'
father, Albert Poole Jacobs, Phi '73, was
a
leading Detroit lawyer, and senior
warden of St. Paul's Cathedral in Detroit.
Unique in fraternity histories is the fact
that the father wrote the first fifty years of
Psi Upsilon, in his Epitome, and the son
completed the history to 1941, in the
Annals of Psi Upsilon. Brother Jacobs has
one sister, Dr. Charlotte B. Newman,
Professor of Bacteriology at Hunter Col
lege, New York City.
He was selected as a Rhodes Scholar
upon his graduation from the University
of Michigan in 1921. At Oxford, he was
named a don, the only American ever to
get a
lecturing fellowship. He stayed in
England for six years as a lecturer in
jurisprudence at Oriel and Brasenose Col
leges while earning the degrees of Bach
elor of Arts in 1923, Bachelor of Civil
Law in 1924, and the Oxford Master of
Arts, considered equivalent of the Amer
ican doctorate, in 1927.
He joined the Columbia University fac
ulty in 1927 as a lecturer in law and was
recognized as an
outstanding teacher be
fore he reached the age of 30, being pro
moted to assistant professor in 1928, and
associate professor in 1929 at the age of
29. He became a full professor in 1936.
His popularity with the faculty was
attested by his election to the presidency
of the Mens' Faculty Club of the Univer
sity for six years from 1934 to 1940. From
1939 to 1942, he was chairman of the
University Committee on Public Cere
monies and in 1942 was chairman of the
Committee on
University Security. Dr.
Jacobs is a
prominent Episcopal layman,
having served while at Columbia as a
member of the Board of ReHgious Educa
tion of the Diocese of New York and chair
man of the Commission on
College Work.
Trinity was founded as a
college for
men of all faiths by Episcopalians in 1823
and has always maintained a close, in
formal relationship with the Episcopal
Church and a
strong emphasis on
spiritual
development in its requirements. Dr.
Jacobs is now a
vestryman of St. John's
Cathedral in Denver of which the Dean is
the Very Rev. Paul Roberts, Beta Beta '09.
Dr. Jacobs' undergraduate study at
Michigan had been interrupted by service
as a
private in World War I. During the
second World War, he was commissioned a
lieutenant commander in the Naval Re
serve in 1942, and rose to captain during

his service as Director of the Casualties
and Dependents Welfare Division of the
Bureau of Naval Personnel in Washington
until November, 1945. Brother Jacobs is
an
authority on
family law. For his out
standing services during World War II, he
was awarded the Legion of Merit by the
Navy Department. He is author of A Re
search of Family Law (with Robert C.
Angell), 1930, Cases and Materials in
Landlord and Tenant (1931, 1941), Cases
and Materials on Domestic Relations
(1933, 1939, 1952, with Prof. Julius Goebel), which are considered bibles of the
legal profession.
Upon his return to Columbia, he was
made Assistant to the President for Vet
erans' Affairs, then Assistant to the Presi
dent for General Academic Administra
tion. When General Eisenhower was
named President of Columbia in 1947,
Dr. Jacobs was made Provost of the Uni
versity. At that time, a
university an
nouncement said that he would be Eisen
hower's "principal assistant" and act as
his "alter ego and successor
during the
President's necessary absences from the
University or in event of any emergency."
Upon announcement of Dr. Jacobs' ap
pointment at Denver, General Eisenhower
said that his "contributions to the Uni
versity and to higher education in general
have been brilhant . . ." and added that
he had been "impressed with his extraordi
nary value to the University ... his record
as a
great university administrator . . .
long an
outstanding teacher of law, an
authority in his field." Of his war service,
the General said that the "Navy placed on
his shoulders great responsibility, which
he discharged with distinction."
As Chancellor of the University of Den
ver since 1949, he has headed the largest
university in the Rocky Mountain area,
and is credited with restoring the Univer
sity to a
position of leadership among in
dependent universities in the West after a
difficult period of post-war adjustment.
The term Chancellor is used in place of
President at the University of Denver.
At Denver, Dr. Jacobs has led extensive
reorganization of both the curriculum and
faculty, reshaped the curriculum of the
Community College to meet the needs of
Denver adults, reorganized the athletic
department under E. E. (Tad) Wieman,
and taken a
leading part in Denver civic
affairs. His commencement addresses won
Freedoms Foundation Awards for the past
two years, and the University of Denver
won the Outstanding Campus Program
Freedoms Foundation Award for 1951.
Brother Jacobs has honorary degrees
from Columbia, Colorado College, Syra
cuse, Temple and the University of Colo
rado. Now, as he is about to leave the
University of Denver, the board of trustees
have conferred upon him the degree of
Doctor of Public Service. A citation read
by Board President Robert W. Selig, on
November 20, in part states, ". . . now
in three years of devoted service in Den
ver
affording the University, the city and
the region an
unparalleled stimulus to
intellectual progress and creative citizen
ship and bringing the entire nation a
greater understanding of the vital impor
tance of independent higher education and
the means for its preservation and prog
ress; architect of freedom, soon
returning
to the East but implanting in the educa
tional, religious, governmental, and busi
ness institutions of the West not only chal
lenging goals and perspectives but also
positive steps for their fuffiUment; good
citizen who shall always have the respect,
admiration and affection of the people of
the West; a scholar, a
gentleman, a
pubhc
servant of the highest sense."
Brother Jacobs was
appointed Chair
man of the 1952 Awards Jury of the Free
doms Foundation, at Valley Forge, which
was founded for "Preserving and Extend
ing the American Way of Lffe."
In 1927, Brother Jacobs married Loretta
Field Beal, of Ann Arbor, a
graduate of
the University of Michigan, '24, and a
daughter of Junius E. Beal, for 32 years a
Regent of that University. The Ella Travis
Beal Residence Hall for Nurses at the Uni
versity is named in honor of Mrs. Jacobs'
mother, for her many decades of loyal
service to the University of Michigan. The
Jacobs' have three children, Loretta, a
graduate of the University of Michigan,

Brother Moyer has brought to the duties

a soldier, newspaperman, lawyer and
former secretary to the late Prime Minister
W. L. Mackenzie King.

stock. He was born at Preston, Ontario,
and is a fifth generation Canadian. He is
the son of the late Dr. Sylvester Moyer
who was a candidate for the Federal
House in 1908 and 1911. He secured his
primary education at Gait, Ontario, and
graduated in 1910 from the Arts Faculty
of the University of Toronto with Honours
in Political Economy.
In his senior year at the University he
edited the student publication Varsity. On

addition to his Senatorial duties, served as
Press Censor for Canada, and later as

Board.
While Brother Moyer's background is
definitely Liberal, he has always enjoyed
a wide popularity on Parhament Hill in
all political circles. His is an
impressive as
well as a
uniformly courteous and genial

quite regardless of pohtical lines. His

public official while secre
tary to Prime Minister King was that of a

capacity for an infinite amount of work
with the minimum of nervous strain upon
the staff associated with it. His appoint
ment to his present position was no less
acceptable to the Conservative members

president. Guaranty's resources exceed

FOUNDERS' DAY CELEBRATED IN NEW YORK
A

held at the Columbia University
Club, New York City, on November 24,
1952. LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01, Presi
dent of the Executive Council, presided
and spoke briefly, as did Brother Herbert
S. Houston, Omega '88, and Senator
Theodore Francis Green, Sigma '87.

ation of Psi Upsilon to some 2,300 mem

Climaxing a

December 13, when we held our annual
Christmas Formal in the beautiful Colonial
Room of the Ambassador Hotel. The day got
off to a
good start as the Brothers initiated
their first pledge class at three-thirty that
afternoon. With the help of the Alumni, six
men were initiated into the mystic bond of
Psi Upsilon. They were Bob Kiem, George
Steffis, Duane Kirkpatrick, Tony Francis,
Roger Watson, and BiU Brink. Bob Kiem was
named outstanding pledge at the dinner
dance, arranged by Brother Bud Lisle.

recently with Brother Frank Ruttencutter
taking the gavel as President, Brother Frank
Kaufinann, Recording Secretary; Pete Vlahos,
Treasurer; Brother Joseph Schneider, VicePresident; and Ken Himes, Corresponding
